toc.title: "But small steps don't feel like enough"
When the overwhelm keeps coming back

blocks.p: Do you feel like you're drowning in to-do lists? Of course you do. We all do. You have small daily things, the basics like showering, brushing your teeth, and eating. You have bigger daily things like childcare, work, and relationships. You have things you have to get done, like taxes and house maintenance. And you have things you would love to do if you just had the space for them: a new hobby, starting a business, joining a club, getting back to the gym.
There's too much to do and not enough time. Things pile up, and you're probably being unkind to yourself about it. If you're overwhelmed, it's because you're normal. You're human.

As you read, look for the moment of "that's it, I can do that." You don't need to remember all of this. Find one thing that sparks you, one goal you want to make progress on and one step toward it, and run with that.
Overwhelm is defensive activation. It can show up in a few ways:

ul: Freeze: feeling stuck or paralyzed, panicky, maybe even rage.
Shutdown: collapse. Limp, no energy. "I don't even have the energy for the basic things, Justin. Stop talking about taxes."
Flight: avoiding it altogether.
Fight: it's somebody else's fault, and they can deal with it. Good luck to them.

blocks.p: That's where we're at. We're all there. So what do we do about it? There are three paths:

ol: Anchor in safety first, so the overwhelm comes down and there's room to get things done.
Soften the defense by meeting it mindfully, before, during, and after.
Go around the overwhelm with steps so small they don't set it off.

blocks.p: As you read about each one, notice which one you feel pulled toward. That pull is worth following.

blocks.h: Path one: anchor in safety first

blocks.p: When your ventral vagal safety pathways are active, you get all the things you'd love to have all the time: clear thinking, calm, motivation, focus, hopeful expectations. When safety comes up, defense tends to come down. Less overwhelm means more room to get things done.
So how do you get more safety? Start with what's around you.

Safety cues are things that bring up your safety state without you having to think about them or do anything special. In my therapy office, the greens in the room cue safety for me, and I think for most of my clients too. Nobody has to think about it. The greens are just there, a steady stream of safety cues.

You can do the same at home by creating a passive safety environment. It doesn't matter if it's a house or an apartment. Is there one corner, one room, one spot where there's more safety than anywhere else? Pick that spot and build it up. Add things that feel good. Take away what doesn't: tidy, clean, organize. One spot where you get more safety cues than danger cues goes a long way.

If you don't have a spot like that, find one. A park. A neighborhood lake. A quiet corner of the library. Your backyard with your pet. Your balcony, looking up at the sky or out at the horizon. These are places you find rather than build, and you can go to them to bring safety up and overwhelm down.

blocks.h3: Turn a cue into a mindful anchor

blocks.p: Passive cues help. Connecting with them on purpose helps more. That's where mindfulness comes in: you bring all your attention to the cue.

I have a citrus candle in my office. When it's lit, the room smells like it. That's passive. When I breathe it in on purpose, now I'm mindfully connecting with it. And I can go further, one step at a time:

ol: Do I like it or not?
When I breathe it in, what happens to my breathing? Is the next breath calmer, lighter, tenser?
What happens in my muscles? Do they relax or tighten?
What happens in my internal sensations? More energy? A flutter? A pull downward? A heaviness?

blocks.p: That's how something passive becomes a mindful safety anchor. It anchors you more than the passive cue does on its own, and the overwhelm tends to come down with it.
Deb Dana put that first question simply when she was on the podcast:

q: It's either a drainer or a filler. It's either going to nourish me or it's not going to nourish me.
blocks.cite: Deb Dana, [Deb Dana: Book 2 and COVID-19 (episode 54)](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/98a53db3-770b-483d-ad74-40256d4c6b3a)

blocks.p: If this is hard for you, that's okay. Stick with the first question: do I like it or not? If you like it, do more of it, as long as it's not harmful. You probably already have plenty to work with: a blanket, tea, going outside, pictures of nature, the sound of waves on your phone, music.

Nadia has a test in three days. She's put off studying, choosing her phone and her friends instead. Her dorm is a mess, and her roommates have people in and out all the time. The pressure is building to the point of overwhelm.

So she decides to anchor in safety before she studies. Her dorm isn't a safe place for her, so she walks to the pond on campus and sits on a bench under a tree. She feels a little calm. She closes her eyes and listens to the ducks, feels the air on her skin, and listens to her thumb flipping the pages of her book. She notices whether she likes these things, what happens to her breathing, what happens in her muscles, and what's happening inside.
Safety first, by turning passive cues into mindful anchors. Now she's a lot more likely to study and actually get something out of it.

blocks.why: This article talks about anchoring in safety. This practice does just that, tuned to you.

blocks.p: The second path is to meet the overwhelm itself. There are three times to do that: before it spikes, while it's happening, and after.

Most of us wait until we're overwhelmed to do something about it. I'd really push you to start before. Deb Dana said it well on the podcast: "What we need to do is to preplan for this, to be proactive." ([Episode 54](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/98a53db3-770b-483d-ad74-40256d4c6b3a)) Overwhelm builds and builds, but some of it is already there. So don't wait for it to spike. Notice what it feels like now.

Anchor in safety, the way Nadia did. Then bring your attention to the stress that's already there, and validate it. That just means acknowledging it, normalizing it, and giving it permission to be with you. You're not feeling into it deeply. That comes later.

You can also anchor in safety and then imagine the overwhelm ahead of time, the moment you know is coming, and mindfully give it permission to be there. That lets you feel into it a little. Acknowledge it, and then come back to safety.

So you shift your attention from that anchored, mindful place to "I do have some stress here. This is what it feels like. This is where it lives in my body." Then you bring your attention back to safety. Doing that back and forth a few times is pendulation. But even once, safety to defense and back to safety, goes a long way.
When the defense is already here, most people cope as best they can. What I recommend is to mindfully permit it:

ol: Normalize it. Does it make sense that it's there? For Nadia, yes: "I haven't studied at all, and I'm running out of time."
Permit it. Give it an image, using your imagination. Then invite it to be there with you while you make progress on what you have to do.

blocks.p: You're not feeling into it here. If the overwhelm is spiking at a seven or eight out of ten, that's probably too much to feel into. You just want to bring it down enough, with imagery and invitation, so you can get some things done.
After the overwhelm, let yourself recover. Actually let yourself come down.

If work was terrible, with stress and people and problems, and you come home still wound up, give yourself time to decompress. Something I love to recommend to my clients: when you get home, fall face first onto your bed. Give yourself ten minutes of silence. Just breathe, and maybe connect with your pet. That little bit of time does far more than coming home and turning on the TV, which isn't restorative.
Of the three, put most of your energy into before and after. During is where you'll get the least benefit, and you have to work your way up to it.
Nadia has already anchored in safety at the pond. Now she softens the defense.
She validates it: "I feel stressed." She normalizes it: "I put it off too long, and this test matters. And my dang roommates. Of course I'm stressed."

Then she permits it by giving her stress an image. What comes to mind is a heavy rock weighing her down. "I'm going to put you here on the bench next to me. Heavy rock, you're invited to hang out with me while I study." Then she opens her textbook and starts reading.
She isn't rejecting the stress. She's giving it permission to be there and using an image to hold it. It doesn't solve the problem. It softens it enough to get things done.

Then she builds on it. Back in her room, which she's set up with things that cue safety for her, she anchors again, maybe with a candle. Then she imagines the test, which is two days away now. She pictures herself at the desk in class, stressed. She lets herself have it, because it's coming anyway. She feels a little of the stress through her imagination, without going too far, and then comes back to safety. She does that a couple of times, pendulating between the two.

That's like putting in reps for anything else. It tells the body: we've felt this level of stress before. We know it, because we practiced it days ahead of time. Practice this way, and when the stress shows up for real, your body recognizes it and can move between it and safety on its own, without you having to think about it.

I see this in my client work, where we practice pendulation at a much heavier intensity. Clients often use a pet as a co-regulator, a point of connection. As they feel defense, I'll ask, "How's your pet doing?" They smile and connect, and that builds their safety state. A session or two later, without any prompting, as they feel defensive activation, their hand goes right to the pet. Their body has learned to anchor in safety while defense is there too.

You can use this anywhere. If the grocery store overwhelms you, practice before you go. Anchor in safety. I like to fidget with my AirPods case; when I focus on it, I feel more anchored. Then imagine the store: the people, the lights, the sounds. Feel a little of it, then come back to safety. Afterward, in the car or at home, decompress. Tell yourself something kind. Let out a long breath.

I do this myself. I'm afraid of heights, so I started a practice of imagining myself falling. It was terrifying at first, and it's gotten easier and easier. Not long ago, I drove over a bridge that used to set me off badly, and it didn't set me off at all, because I'd been putting in the mental reps ahead of time. In the store, or on the bridge, the fear is still there, but it's not what it used to be. It's far more manageable.

blocks.h: Path three: go around the overwhelm with kaizen

blocks.p: Kaizen means good change: kai means change, and zen means good. It was popularized as a Japanese business philosophy of continuous improvement, though it actually came from America during World War II, was exported to Japan, where they took off with it, and then we kind of lost it. It's small steps that build sustainable habits toward a larger goal. I love it, and I build it into my own life.

Here's why it works. The things you want to accomplish set off defense. Life's tasks, even brushing your teeth for some people, and your goals, like joining a gym, trigger defensive activation. Change is scary, period. Even change you want. And a daily task that seems like it should be easy, like showering every day, might be too much if it's a new habit, especially if you're stuck in a defensive state.

Kaizen finds behaviors so small they don't set off fear, panic, or overwhelm. You can use it when you're already overwhelmed, but it works best when you use it proactively, while your emotional state is more manageable.

A kaizen step should be so small that it doesn't trigger defense at all. So small it isn't a challenge. You should be 99% confident you can do it. It might even seem silly. When my clients and I come up with kaizen goals, they often laugh: "Yeah, I can do that. That's silly. Of course I can." That's what we want. There's no friction, just momentum. Then do it again the next day.
No step is too small:

ul: Thirty seconds is better than none, whether it's walking, exercise, or mindfulness.
Five reps is better than no reps.
One minute of planning is a step toward doing.
Imagining your goal is better than avoiding it. A vision board is better than nothing, and a few notes in a notebook are better than no vision board.
Walking around the block is better than not going to the gym. Walking halfway around is better than nothing. Putting your shoes on and walking to the front door is better than nothing too.

blocks.h3: Four questions to find your step

blocks.p: Pick one of these and match it to a goal:

ol: What is the smallest step I can take now to move closer to my goal?
How can I make it feel effortless, even enjoyable?
What's one simple way to fit it into my existing routine?
What small action needs to happen before I can move forward?

blocks.p: Here's how they worked for a mindfulness challenge I ran in my community. If I'd said, "You're going to practice mindfulness twenty days in a row," good luck. That's overwhelming. So I built kaizen into it.

ul: Smallest step: about thirty seconds a day, each day a little more challenging. Day one, use your sense of smell and notice whether you like or dislike something. Day two, notice how a smell affects your breathing. Then your muscle tension. Then whether you're more or less likely to smile. Then the sensations in your body. Five days per sense, four senses.
Effortless and enjoyable: we did it together, as a community. I did it too, and I loved it.

Fits the routine: it's thirty seconds. Some days I forgot until a notification popped up that someone else had done it. "Oops. Thirty seconds. I'm not behind." I was on my couch, so I mindfully touched the couch with my hand for thirty seconds. Done.
Small action first: on day zero, anyone who wanted in typed "I'm in." That got the ball rolling.

blocks.p: Tatiana wants to start an origami hobby, but she's put it off forever. Every time she thinks about starting, she thinks about leaving the house, going to the art store, dealing with people, spending money. It seems like a small goal, just buy paper, but for someone stuck in defense, every step is a "no."
Her goal is an origami hobby. A smaller goal is origami three times a week, and that might still be too much. Her kaizen goal: fold a piece of paper every day.

ul: Smallest step: find one sheet of paper, any paper, even a sticky note, and fold it.
Effortless: keep it in her pocket. You can fold paper anywhere.
Fits her routine: fold it while watching TV, in the elevator, while cooking.
Small action first: find that first piece of paper now. That's it.

blocks.p: James wants to lose weight and build muscle, but he's put it off for years, prioritizing work and family. The thought of the gym makes him feel overwhelmed, self-conscious, and exhausted before he starts. He worries about the time, the effort, keeping up, the money. He doesn't want to feel alone and insecure.
The goal setting off his defense is the gym. A smaller goal might be a home gym, but that could be overwhelming and expensive too. A kaizen goal could be a walk every day.

ul: Smallest step: a walk, lifting a milk jug, picking up his kids.
Effortless and enjoyable: walk with his family, maybe make a game of it.
Fits his routine: walk around the office during phone calls, park farther from the entrance, stand up during non-screen time at work.
Small action first: ask his family to join him, email HR about a standing desk, or find something around the house to lift.

blocks.h3: Heather and going back to school

blocks.p: Heather wants to go back to school, but she's overwhelmed by balancing work, school, and life, and unsure about the money and time.

Her goal is returning to school. A smaller goal might be a short course. A kaizen goal: get the wheels moving. Read a book on the subject, watch a video, listen to a podcast. Spend two minutes looking up one program. The next day, two minutes on another. Visit a school's website. Look at a course catalog. Talk to people already taking short courses.

We wouldn't tell Heather to register, do all the research, and figure everything out now. That's too much. She's already overwhelmed, and it's a huge change. But looking at one program now? She'd probably say, "Yeah, I can handle that. That's easy." That's the point. The overwhelm isn't an issue anymore, because the step is laughably easy.

As you start taking kaizen steps, you'll find they snowball. Once you do the first one, you'll think, "That was silly. That was easy. I can totally do that again." I see it in my business. There are things in the back of my mind I want to get to, and then I don't. But I have an accountability partner. We each set our goals, and once I come up with a small one and nail it, I think, "I could totally do the next thing," and it unravels from there. That first step is where kaizen is huge.

blocks.h: "But small steps don't feel like enough"

blocks.p: A common reaction: "Logically I get baby steps, but emotionally it doesn't feel like enough. I have a deadline. I can't afford to go slow."

If there's real time pressure, that makes it harder. Say someone with social anxiety feels they need to be married by a certain age, but big steps make them spiral, freeze, and shut down. Where your mind goes is where everybody's goes. Mine went there too when I first heard this. "Yeah, I get it, but come on, that's not the answer."

That reaction makes sense, and it comes up all the time with my clients. My response is: I agree with you. But right now you're not doing anything at all. So let's take a baby step. What's the other option, to keep saying "I need more" and not do anything?

It might help to shift "I have to" into "I want to." Then ask what's possible now. Finding the perfect partner now is probably too much. But could you go to something in person, a local meetup, a biking club, something you're into where you're likely to meet people with similar interests? Even with a huge goal and a lot of pressure, the principle holds. A step forward now is better than none.

I had a client with a lot of anxiety who wanted to get outside more. A daily walk wasn't happening. So we asked, "Can you put your shoes on and walk to the front door?" Even that was too much. But now she practices mindfulness regularly, in small increments, as part of her normal day, and she's doing a lot better. She can welcome waves of anxiety as they come and go, and sit with them far more easily. She's a lot more proactive.

blocks.h: When the overwhelm keeps coming back

blocks.p: Some overwhelm is built into life, like a busy season at work, or a project that overwhelms you between every step. For that, lean on path two more than path three. Work is work, and you have to get through it. Consistently bringing overwhelm down will help more than hunting for the perfect kaizen goal.

ul: Before: can you feel a bit more safety or mindfulness before work, as a buffer for everything that's coming?
During: can you take small breaks between tasks and truly decompress, not on your phone, not answering one more email, just breathing?
After: can you truly decompress after work? Flop, and be in silence for five or ten minutes.

blocks.p: Then ask: how can I streamline this? What's one small change that would make my life a little easier?

For me, it's a three-box system. Box one is everything I don't like doing but have to do: progress notes, treatment plans, paperwork, anything that isn't therapy or creative. Box two is what I like doing: podcasting, writing, creating coursework. Box three is what I love doing that has no short-term payoff, like tweaking design on my site. I can't move to box two until box one is done.

Your space matters too. It's important to me that my therapy office and home office are decluttered, with visual space and physical space, and things organized. Not compulsively or obsessively clean, but tidy. When I walk in, I want to feel like I can focus. If I need something, I know where it is, and I get back to work. Little changes like that can release a lot of overwhelm.

What's one thing you want to achieve, work toward, or improve? If it's showering daily, that's fine. If it's joining a bike club or starting a business, that's great too. Don't try to answer all of these. If one speaks to you, latch onto it.

ul: What simple or daily things are you putting off?
Is there a person or a place that's been calling to you? You don't have to book the cruise. Just take a step in that direction.
Is there a big thing you want to take on: a hobby, a project, a business, an adventure?
Is there a movement that would feel good: walking, jogging, singing?

blocks.p: Then answer one of the four questions. You don't need the perfect kaizen goal right now, just a step toward one. If your goal is woodworking, do you have the wood and the tools? If not, is it time to order them? If that's too much, can you imagine woodworking, just put yourself in that space? Visualizing it is a step in the right direction.

If you already have a space for it, are you more likely to spend one minute there than zero? Can you walk in, touch the things, connect with them, and say, "I'll be here tomorrow for one minute"? Can you walk through that space on your way to the car? If you can do thirty seconds, I'd be ecstatic for you.
The journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step.
